content: Lck, also known as lymphocyte-specific protein tyrosine kinase, is a 56-kilodalton protein predominantly found in lymphocytes, which are specialized cells of the immune system. It functions as a tyrosine kinase, meaning it phosphorylates tyrosine residues on specific proteins that are integral to intracellular signaling pathways within these lymphocytes. Lck is a member of the Src family of tyrosine kinases. In T cells, Lck is primarily associated with the cytoplasmic tails of the CD4 and CD8 co-receptors. These co-receptors are present on T helper cells and cytotoxic T cells, respectively. Lck plays a critical role in facilitating signal transduction from the T cell receptor (TCR) complex. When the TCR engages with a specific antigen presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), Lck phosphorylates the intracellular chains of the CD3 and ζ-chains of the TCR complex. This phosphorylation creates binding sites for another cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, ZAP-70. Lck subsequently phosphorylates and activates ZAP-70, which then phosphorylates a transmembrane protein called LAT (Linker of Activated T cells). LAT serves as a docking site for several other signaling proteins, including Shc-Grb2-SOS, PI3K, and phospholipase C (PLC). Upon T cell activation, a portion of active Lck translocates from outside lipid rafts to within lipid rafts, where it interacts with and activates Fyn, another Src family kinase. This interaction contributes to further downstream signaling activation. The tyrosine phosphorylation cascade initiated by Lck and Fyn ultimately leads to intracellular calcium (Ca2+) mobilization and the activation of key signaling pathways, such as the Ras-MEK-ERK pathway. These pathways activate transcription factors like NFAT, NF-κB, and AP-1, which regulate the expression of numerous genes, including cytokines like interleukin-2 (IL-2). IL-2 is essential for the long-term proliferation and differentiation of activated lymphocytes. Structurally, Lck is a 56-kilodalton protein with an N-terminal tail that is myristoylated and palmitoylated, anchoring it to the plasma membrane. It contains an SH3 domain, an SH2 domain, and a tyrosine kinase domain in its C-terminal region. Two key phosphorylation sites on Lck are tyrosines 394 and 505. Tyrosine 394 is an autophosphorylation site linked to the activation of Lck, while tyrosine 505 is phosphorylated by Csk, which inhibits Lck by causing the protein to fold and bind its own SH2 domain. This dual regulation exemplifies how protein phosphorylation can result in both activation and inhibition. Lck phosphorylates several substrates, including the CD3 receptor, CEACAM1, ZAP-70, SLP-76, the IL-2 receptor, protein kinase C, ITK, PLC, Shc, RasGAP, Cbl, Vav1, and PI3K. In resting T cells, Lck is constitutively inhibited by Csk-mediated phosphorylation of tyrosine 505. It is also inhibited by SHP-1, which dephosphorylates tyrosine 394, and by Cbl ubiquitin ligase, which is part of the ubiquitin-mediated degradation pathway. Pharmacological inhibitors of Lck, such as saracatinib, impair the maintenance of human T-ALL (T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia) cells both in vitro and in vivo by targeting this tyrosine kinase in cells with high levels of lipid rafts. Masitinib also inhibits Lck and may contribute to its therapeutic effects in canine mastocytoma. Lck has been shown to interact with several proteins, including ADAM15, CD2, CD44, CD4, COUP-TFII, DLG1, NOTCH1, PIK3CA, PTPN6, PTPRC, UNC119, SYK, UBE3A, and ZAP-70.
